c.v: A robot stands at x = 4 m, y = 1 m in the world frame, with a yaw of 90°: it faces along the world's y axis. Its lidar reports a point 2 m ahead of the robot and 0.5 m to its left, which is (2, 0.5) in the robot's frame. By hand, find the point in the world frame, and write down the 3×3 homogeneous matrix you used. Take 10 minutes.
Turn the point by the robot's yaw, then add the robot's position:
Check it in words: 2 m ahead is 2 m along the world's y axis, so y goes from 1 to 3, and the robot's left is the world's −x, so x goes from 4 to 3.5.

You pass with (3.5, 3.0), the rule "rotate, then translate", and the matrix. A sign slip with the right method is a partial pass: (4.5, 3.0) comes from a wrong sign on one sine term, and (4.5, −1.0) from turning by −90° instead of +90°. Adding the offsets without rotating, which gives (6.0, 1.5), is a fail.

A frame is an origin and a set of axes, and a pose is the position and orientation of one frame stated in another: the same physical point has different coordinates depending on which frame describes it. ROS names the robot's own frame
and the world frame of a mobile robot
, and every message that carries a position, such as
, names the frame those numbers are stated in, because the numbers alone say nothing.

The problem is that a sensor reading, stated in the frame of the sensor, is useless to anything reasoning about the world unless there is a defined way to restate it in another frame. Adding a robot's position straight to a reading taken relative to the robot gives a wrong point whenever the robot doesn't face the world's own axes, because the reading's directions are the robot's, not the world's.

The fix is to turn the reading into the target frame's directions before adding the target frame's position: a rotation matrix does the turning, its columns being the child frame's axes written in the parent's, and a homogeneous transform packs rotation and translation into one matrix, so a chain of frames becomes one matrix product. Naming a transform target-first,
, keeps the direction straight: the inner names of a correct chain,
, must meet, and a mismatch there is the only warning you get. The inverse swaps source and target with no general matrix inversion, since a rotation's inverse is its own transpose.

What this costs you is the discipline to say what kind of thing you are transforming. A point has a place and moves with translation; a vector, a velocity or an offset between two points, has only a direction and length and must only be turned, never moved, which homogeneous coordinates enforce by giving a point's fourth coordinate 1 and a vector's 0. Treating a velocity as a point silently adds the robot's own position to it, producing a place instead of a speed, with nothing to catch the mistake but the answer looking wrong.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself: turning a lidar reading stated in the robot's own frame into the world frame by rotating first and translating second, exactly the discipline REP 105 relies on when it splits a robot's world position into

Take the cold check's robot at (4, 1), facing along the world's y axis, and a lidar return 2 m straight ahead. Adding the numbers gives (6, 1), a point 2 m along the world's x axis, off to the robot's right. The right answer is (4, 3). "Ahead" means the robot's x axis, and that axis points along the world's y axis, so the reading has to be turned into the world's directions before the robot's position is added.

is an origin and a set of axes. The obstacle has coordinates (2, 0) in the robot's frame and (4, 3) in the world frame: the point is the same, only the frame that describes it differs. That is why ROS messages that carry positions and velocities name their frames:
. ROS calls the world frame of a mobile robot
Turning coordinates from a child frame into its parent is a multiplication by a
. For a child frame turned by the yaw θ against its parent:

blocks.text:
R(θ) = | cos θ  −sin θ |          p_parent = R(θ) · p_child + t
       | sin θ   cos θ |

c.v: Here t is the child's origin in parent coordinates. Read R by its columns: the first column, (cos θ, sin θ), is the child's x axis written in the parent frame, and the second, (−sin θ, cos θ), is its y axis. For the robot, θ = 90°, so its x axis is (0, 1) in the map, and 2 m ahead is 2·(0, 1) + (4, 1) = (4, 3).

Two properties of rotation matrices come up constantly. Their columns have length 1 and are at right angles, so the inverse of R is its transpose, and R(θ)ᵀ = R(−θ). And their determinant is +1. A matrix with determinant −1 mirrors, which turns a right-handed frame into a left-handed one, and every ROS frame is right-handed.
Carrying R and t separately gets clumsy once frames chain. The lidar has a frame of its own,
, mounted somewhere on the robot, so a scan point goes from
packs R and t into one 3×3 matrix and gives each point a third coordinate, 1:

blocks.text:
| x_map |   | cos θ  −sin θ  t_x |   | x_base |
| y_map | = | sin θ   cos θ  t_y | · | y_base |
|   1   |   |   0       0     1  |   |   1    |

c.v: Multiply it out and the first two rows are R·p + t, while the last row keeps the 1. Now a chain of frames is a product of matrices, and the product of two such matrices is again one of them, so any chain collapses into a single transform.
This page names a transform after its two frames, target first.

The inner names, base and base, match and drop out. Lynch and Park call this the

tf2 stores the same thing under different words. A
returns it: the first argument is the frame the data should end up in (
). REP 105 calls it "the transform from map to base_link", naming parent then child, although it converts coordinates the other way. Variable names in the
The inverse turns the direction around:

. The common guess is (−x, −y, −θ), which puts the map's origin at (−4, −1) in the robot's frame. Work it out instead. From the robot, the map's origin is 4 m along the map's −x axis, which is the robot's left, and 1 m along the map's −y axis, which is behind it. So it sits at (−1, 4) in the robot's frame. The formula for the inverse of a rigid transform gives the same:
No general matrix inversion is needed: the transpose takes no arithmetic and adds no rounding (Modern Robotics, proposition 3.15).
A point has a place. A

has a direction and a length and no place: a velocity, the offset from one point to another, the direction a camera looks. Moving a frame's origin changes the coordinates of every point in it and of no vector. Homogeneous coordinates keep the two apart with the last coordinate: a point gets 1 and a vector gets 0, and the 0 cancels the translation column, so a transform only turns a vector. The robot's forward velocity of 0.5 m/s is (0.5, 0) in

. Treated as a point, it would come out as (4, 1.5), which is a place and not a velocity. The difference of two points is a vector, a point plus a vector is a point, and a point plus a point has no meaning.

Re-expressing a velocity in another frame's axes is a rotation. The velocity of a different point on a turning robot, such as the lidar, is a different quantity: it adds the turn rate times the lever arm.
ROS messages make the same split.

Nothing above depends on the plane. In 3D, R is 3×3, t has three entries, the homogeneous transform is 4×4 with 0 0 0 1 as its last row, and a point is (x, y, z, 1). Composition, the inverse with Rᵀ and −Rᵀ·t, and the 0 for vectors all carry over unchanged. A turn by yaw about z is the 2D matrix with a 1 added for z:

blocks.text:
Rz(θ) = | cos θ  −sin θ  0 |
        | sin θ   cos θ  0 |
        |   0       0    1 |

c.v: The column rule still holds: each column of R is one axis of the child frame, written in the parent frame. That is often the fastest way to write a rotation down, and the worked example does so for a camera. Rotations about x and y, and the quaternions that ROS messages use for orientation, are the next topic.
A correct formula still gives wrong answers when the data arrives in other units or axes.

c.v: The last two rows differ from habits outside ROS. A compass heading is 0 at north and grows clockwise, while a ROS yaw is 0 at east and grows counterclockwise, so yaw = 90° − heading, and REP 103 asks drivers to convert before they publish. An image has x to the right and y down, so points seen by a camera are described in its optical frame, and a fixed rotation connects that frame to the camera's body frame.

This program follows one point from a camera to the map, in 3D. The robot is at (4, 1) in the map, facing along the map's y axis. Its camera sits 0.1 m ahead of

and 0.3 m up, and the camera describes what it sees in its optical frame. It sees a point 2 m in front of the lens, 0.5 m right of the image centre and 0.2 m below it, so (0.5, 0.2, 2.0) in the optical frame.
Work out the answer before running it. The point is 2 m ahead of the camera, which is 0.1 m ahead of
, so it is 2.1 m along the map's y axis from the robot: y = 3.1. Right of a robot facing +y is +x, so x = 4.5. The height is 0.3 m minus 0.2 m, so z = 0.1.

items.v: Three steps and one chained transform give the same point. The chain collapsed into a single matrix, which is what tf2 hands you when a lookup crosses several frames.
Nobody wrote the rotation block of

; the product built it. Read it by columns: the optical x axis, right in the image, is the map's +x; the optical y axis, down in the image, is the map's −z; and the optical z axis, where the camera looks, is the map's +y. The last column, (4.0, 1.1, 0.3), is the camera's position in the map.

The same three numbers mean different things as a vector and as a point. With w = 0, the optical z axis comes out as (0, 1, 0), the direction the camera looks. With w = 1, it is (4.0, 2.1, 0.3), the place 1 m in front of the lens.
The inverse, built from the transpose, brings the map point back to (0.5, 0.2, 2.0).
The wrong order runs without complaint and prints a plausible point. Its inner names don't meet: optical against base, and camera against map. The names are the only check there is.
